rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

All pairs have resolution to spare, so halve the gradient duration to shorten the run. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed will reveal which critical pairs lose resolution as the gradient steepens.

Use an intermediate gradient duration to recover resolution in the compressed central cluster while keeping the last peak near nine minutes. This tests whether slope adjustment alone can approach full resolution without a time penalty.

Keep the promising gradient slope and raise temperature to test selectivity in the remaining critical pair. Faster elution should preserve the zero time penalty, while a modest selectivity shift may bring every pair above R = 1.5.

The central retention pattern suggests the critical pair crossed between 40 and 50 C; another 5 C increase may separate it again. Keep the gradient fixed to test this while monitoring the neighboring pair that narrowed at 50 C.

Slightly steepen the gradient at the best temperature to separate the central pair further after its apparent elution-order reversal. This modest slope change should retain adequate resolution for the neighboring pair and keep the time penalty at zero.

Injection 6 reached the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark. A small increase in gradient steepness tests a faster alternative that may give the critical pair slightly more resolution while keeping its neighboring pair above 1.5.

The maximum CRF is already secured. Raise the starting organic fraction slightly to test whether shifting the gradient window can shorten elution while improving the narrow resolution margins of the two closest pairs.

Reduce the gradient slope to restore resolution of the pair that narrowed in injection 8, while retaining the improved separation of the other critical pair. The last peak should remain inside the gradient with no time penalty, potentially giving a maximum-score method with better resolution margins.

Test a narrower gradient window to improve the resolution margins of the maximum-score method from injection 9. The shallower slope should offset compression from the higher starting organic fraction, with all peaks expected to elute before the time penalty begins.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope relative to injection 10 to improve its limiting pair while aiming to keep the last peak below ten minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured; this tests a method with a larger minimum-resolution margin.

With the maximum CRF already secured, explore a substantially faster alternative using higher temperature and a steeper gradient. These changes may carry the narrowing middle pair through an elution-order reversal and restore separation, though this is an exploratory run.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to move the newly reversed middle pair farther apart while maintaining a short run. This explores a faster maximum-score alternative; the established CRF 1.000 methods remain the benchmarks.

Continue shifting the starting composition to test whether the reversed critical pair can reach baseline resolution in a sub-five-minute separation. Monitor both the early pair and the neighboring central pair, which may become limiting as the starting organic fraction rises.

Return to the maximum-score region and slightly flatten injection 9’s gradient to improve its tighter neighboring separation. This should preserve baseline resolution of the critical central pair and keep the last peak below ten minutes.

Fine-tune the slope between injections 10 and 11 to balance their two limiting pairs near R = 1.7. This targets a larger minimum-resolution margin while preserving the maximum CRF and a last-peak time below ten minutes.

Test a shallower gradient at 60 C to separate the middle pair on the opposite side of its crossover from the fast runs. The higher temperature should strengthen separation of the other critical pair, potentially yielding another maximum-score method with wider resolution margins.

Return to 55 C and use a slope between injections 9 and 15, where both critical pairs were baseline resolved. This should preserve the maximum CRF with a last-peak time near eight minutes and modest resolution margins.

Slightly steepen the gradient relative to injection 10 to shorten the run while targeting baseline resolution of both critical pairs. This refines the established maximum-score region without repeating a method.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 15 to increase separation of its neighboring central pair while checking that the limiting pair remains above R = 1.5. This stays near the established maximum-score region, with the last peak expected before nine minutes.

Use a narrower solvent window with nearly the same slope as injection 16, targeting its balanced resolution margins and maximum CRF. The last peak is expected near 9.3 minutes, still within the programmed gradient.

Slightly steepen injection 9’s gradient to seek a shorter maximum-score separation while retaining baseline resolution of both critical pairs. The last peak should elute near 7.8 minutes, comfortably within the gradient and below the time-penalty threshold.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 11 to check the resolution margin around the balanced method from injection 16. All peaks should remain within the gradient, with the last peak below ten minutes and CRF at its maximum.

Extend the shallow-slope edge of the maximum-score region, aiming to retain baseline resolution while keeping the last peak just below ten minutes. This tests the remaining time margin around the well-resolved 55 C methods without repeating a previous method.

Use an untested slope close to injection 19, targeting baseline resolution of both critical pairs and a last-peak time near nine minutes. This final refinement is expected to preserve the maximum CRF without repeating a method.
